title: Three Air India Employees Under Investigation in Amritsar Airport Trafficking Probe
excerpt: A human trafficking investigation at Amritsar's international airport has placed three airline staffers among 29 suspects under scrutiny, highlighting the role of airport insiders in Punjab's illegal migration crisis.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Three Air India employees are among 29 suspects in a human trafficking investigation at Amritsar airport.
  • The probe targets the use of forged documents and irregular check-in procedures for smuggling passengers.
  • Punjab is a major hub for illegal migration, with multiple agencies investigating trafficking networks.
  • This case follows similar airport trafficking incidents at Delhi and Hyderabad airports.

Three Air India employees are among 29 individuals under investigation in a human trafficking probe centered on Sri Guru Ram Das Jee International Airport in Amritsar, according to a Hindustan Times report that shines fresh light on the role of airline insiders in facilitating illegal migration from Punjab.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=7hYnu1gruC8

Airline Insiders Under Scanner

The investigation at Amritsar airport — Punjab's primary international gateway — has placed three Air India employees among a larger group of 29 suspects under the gaze of law enforcement agencies. The probe centers on allegations that airport personnel facilitated the movement of passengers using forged or irregular travel documents, exploiting their insider access to bypass standard immigration and security checks.

The involvement of airline staff in trafficking operations is not unprecedented. In a high-profile case at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport, four AISATS employees — a subsidiary of Air India parent Tata Group — were arrested alongside a UK-bound passenger after CISF personnel uncovered a scheme involving forged Biometric Residence Permits. Staff confessed to receiving payments of ₹40,000 to ₹80,000 per passenger for processing check-ins with fraudulent documents.

Punjab's Trafficking Crisis

The Amritsar investigation reflects a broader crisis in Punjab, which has emerged as one of India's primary hubs for illegal migration. Economic pressures, a strong aspiration for overseas opportunities, and an entrenched network of travel agents and facilitators have combined to create what enforcement agencies describe as a deeply rooted trafficking ecosystem.

"The SIT has been directed to take appropriate action as per law and facts and take action against any person found involved in committing illegalities and indulging in illegal migration and human trafficking."

— Punjab DGP Gaurav Yadav, on the state's anti-trafficking efforts

Punjab Police have previously constituted special investigation teams to probe trafficking networks, particularly following the high-profile grounding of a Nicaragua-bound flight carrying 276 Indian passengers in France in December 2023. The National Investigation Agency has also pursued multiple cases linked to the so-called "donkey route" — the perilous, multi-country path used to smuggle migrants to the United States and Europe.

Airport Security Under Scrutiny

The case raises pointed questions about security protocols at Indian airports, particularly the vetting of airline personnel with access to sensitive check-in and boarding systems. Investigators across multiple cases have found that trafficking networks specifically target ground staff and check-in agents, offering payments to process passengers with forged documents at crew counters or through manual overrides.

India's aviation regulator, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation, is already under pressure over conflict-of-interest concerns. A Reuters investigation published this week revealed that the Ministry of Civil Aviation has repeatedly challenged the DGCA since mid-2025 over officials' relatives securing jobs at airlines, including Air India, raising broader questions about oversight and accountability.

Impact on the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, airport-based trafficking operations carry a dual concern. Legitimate travelers from Punjab — many of whom hold valid work visas, student visas, or permanent residency abroad — face increased scrutiny at immigration counters as authorities tighten checks. Meanwhile, the victims of trafficking networks, often young men from rural Punjab lured by promises of overseas employment, risk exploitation, detention, and deportation.

According to US Customs and Border Protection data, the number of Indians caught attempting to enter the United States illegally tripled over a three-year period, reaching nearly 97,000 between October 2022 and September 2023. Many originated from Punjab and Gujarat.

What's Next

The investigation remains ongoing, with authorities expected to determine whether the 29 suspects operated as part of an organized syndicate or through independent facilitator networks. The outcome could prompt wider reforms to airport staffing protocols and document verification systems at India's international gateways.
